newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-OFFICIALS DECLINE COMMENT ON BECKER TAX REPORT.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-OFFICIALS DECLINE COMMENT ON BECKER TAX REPORT.

text.p: German finance officials declined to comment on Friday on a newspaper report that tax inspectors had searched tennis star Boris Becker's home and removed several documents.

The Bild daily said four tax inspectors had arrived at Becker's house in Munich on Thursday morning with a search warrant. They were admitted to the house although Becker was on holiday in Florida, the paper said in a front-page report.
Munich tax authorities said they never commented on measures undertaken as part of their investigations. Becker's Munich-based manager was unavailable for comment.
Bild said the investigators were probing the period between 1990 and 1993, when Becker lived in Monte Carlo.

The report was published on the same day as a television station released extracts of an interview with Becker, in which he indicated he would leave Germany when his three-year old son was of school age to allow him to lead a more normal life.
"My son Noah won't go to school in Germany," Becker told private broadcaster Sat1.
He added, though, that a move was not imminent. "I'll pay my taxes in Germany next year," he said.
Germany has been rocked by a series of high-profile tax cases involving well-known personalities over the past couple of years.
Peter Graf, father of world women's tennis number one Steffi Graf, is on trial charged with evading 19 million marks ($12.2 million) of tax on his daughter's earnings between 1989 and 1993.

One of the country's top talk show hosts, Margarethe Schreinemakers, was momentarily blacked out in August when she tried to broadcast an item on her own spat with tax authorities, whom she accuses of deducting too much from her income.
